title: Fletcher Henderson's mistakes, and the band leaving Chick Webb on the road
summary: Snowden led the band out after a raise was refused despite threats, later lost a Chrysler to repossession at Small's, and Bushell did some arranging.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: salary, but I averaged -- and we worked seven nights a week, too, you see, and you had $130, $140, $150.00 a week. You could figure on that. And that was right during the depression. The depression started in '30, you know, because the crash was in '29, and that was in '30 when things were rough. Musicians were hungry. But we had that job -- so, something happened. Snowden- told him we wanted a raise. Said he wouldn't give it to us. So, we said, "Well, we quit." Snowden gave him his notice. So, it's time to quit, this gangster -- Harry Lyons said, "You better not take that band out of here." Snowden said, "What do you mean?" "You better not take them out of here. If you do, you'll find yourself in the gutter." Snowden said, "All right, you'll see." Snowden had already told us, "When I give you a signal, have your horns packed." I gave the signal -- we had our horns packed sitting on thestand. And when we finished that night, "You better not take these instruments out of here." So, Snowden said, "Well, we're going to take them out and we're going to quit." And we walked out of the place -- the guy threatened us, said, "Youse won't get up town. I'm going to dump you in the river before you get up town." Snowden said, "Well, start dumping." Snowden always had a pistol in his pocket. Snowden had more nerve than anybody I've ever seen. Had the guts of a mountain lion. The -- one of the greatest guys I know. We were like brothers. We even bought automobiles in partnership. We bought -- one night

we're sitting on the job -- I was his straw boss when we were playing at Small's Paradise. A guy came in, "Who's got the keys to that blue Chrysler out there?" "Who wants to know?" "Finance." Snowden said, "You got them, Garvin?" "No, I forgot them." He looked at me -- he knew I had the keys. Snowden says, "No, he don't have the keys." He said, "Well, I'm going to haul it, I'm going to take it away." And sure enough, they took our Chrysler away from us, right while we were on the job. We were making money -- the salary was $50.00 a week, but I made tips -- I used to lend money to him because I had a little bank roll I got from Hot Feet, you know. I used to lend waiters this money and charge 10 percent interest and all that. And, but we were -- I tell you I didn't start realizing that I had an obligation to try to save money until I was about 45, 50 year old. I was throwing it away and having a ball.
But unfortunately, that band was never recorded?

Never recorded. Snowden was a great banjo player, you know. He came from Baltimore and Washington where all the banjo players came from in those days. Great banjo players of the country came from Baltimore.
Did you do any arranging for that group?
Yes, I did for the shows and I did some of the arrangements we played at Smalls. We had -- Al Sears was with us. We had -- anybody that you might know now -- no,
